stem: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, which observation shows that most of the volume of an atom is empty space?

options.content: Most alpha particles pass through the foil undeflected or with very small deflections.
options.rationale: Correct: they meet nothing that repels them strongly.

options.content: A very small fraction of alpha particles rebound from the foil.
options.rationale: This shows a small, massive, charged nucleus, not that the atom is mostly empty.

options.content: Some alpha particles are deflected through large angles.
options.rationale: Large deflections show concentrated positive charge.

options.content: The alpha particles are slowed down by collisions with air molecules before they ever reach the foil.
options.rationale: This is why the apparatus is evacuated; it says nothing about atoms in the foil.

explanation: If most particles go straight through, they pass far from any concentrated charge or mass: most of the atom is empty space.

stem: Why did a very few alpha particles rebound through more than 90° from the gold foil?

options.content: They passed close to a tiny region holding the positive charge and most of the mass.
options.rationale: Correct: only a massive, highly charged nucleus can turn back a fast alpha particle.

options.content: They collided head-on with electrons, which carry most of the mass of the atom.
options.rationale: Electrons are about 1/7000 of the alpha particle's mass and cannot turn it back.

options.content: They were attracted back by negative charge that is spread evenly through the whole atom.
options.rationale: Alpha particles are repelled by the positive nucleus; spread charge gives weak fields.

options.content: They were reflected by the flat surface of the foil, as light is from a mirror.
options.rationale: The particles penetrate the foil; the deflection is by individual nuclei.

explanation: A very strong repulsion from a tiny, massive, positive nucleus is needed to reverse a fast alpha particle.

stem: How many neutrons are in a nucleus of ${}^{238}_{92}\text{U}$?

options.rationale: This is the number of protons.
This is the total number of nucleons.
Neutrons are A − Z, not A + Z.
Correct: 238 − 92.

stem: Which pair of nuclides are isotopes of the same element?

options.rationale: Same nucleon number but different proton numbers: different elements.
Different proton numbers, so different elements.
Same nucleon number, different proton numbers.
Correct: same proton number, different nucleon numbers.

explanation: Isotopes have the same number of protons and different numbers of neutrons.

stem: Which is the best estimate of the ratio radius of an atom ÷ radius of its nucleus?

options.rationale: Correct: about 10⁻¹⁰ m ÷ 10⁻¹⁴ m.
Far too small: the nucleus would then fill a noticeable fraction of the atom.
Too large: nuclei are about 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m, not 10⁻¹⁸ m.
This is roughly the ratio of volumes, not radii.

explanation: Atomic radius ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m, nuclear radius ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m, so the ratio is about 10⁴ to 10⁵.

stem: In the reaction ${}^{27}_{13}\text{Al} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He} \rightarrow {}^{30}_{15}\text{P} + \text{X}$, what is X?

options.content: a proton
options.rationale: A proton has Z = 1; charge would not balance.

options.content: an alpha particle
options.rationale: That would need A = 4 and Z = 2.

options.content: a neutron
an electron
options.rationale: An electron has A = 0, but the nucleon numbers need 1 more on the right.

explanation: Nucleon number: 31 = 30 + A gives A = 1. Charge: 15 = 15 + Z gives Z = 0. X is a neutron.
hints: Balance the top numbers and the bottom numbers separately.

stem: What is the charge on a nucleus of ${}^{197}_{79}\text{Au}$?

options.rationale: This uses the nucleon number; neutrons are uncharged.
Correct: Ze with Z = 79.
This counts the neutrons, which carry no charge.
The nucleus is positive; the electrons around it carry −79e.

hints: Only protons carry charge in the nucleus.

stem: The gold foil in the scattering experiment is replaced by an aluminium foil of the same thickness. Aluminium nuclei have a much smaller charge. How does the number of alpha particles scattered through large angles change?

options.content: It increases, because aluminium is less dense, so the particles travel further.
options.rationale: Large-angle scattering depends on close encounters with charged nuclei, not on range.

options.content: It decreases, because the repulsive force near each nucleus is weaker.
options.rationale: Correct: smaller nuclear charge gives smaller deflections.

options.content: It is unchanged, because the foil has the same thickness.
options.rationale: Thickness is matched, but the force from each nucleus is smaller.

options.content: It increases, because aluminium nuclei are lighter and recoil more.
options.rationale: Lighter nuclei recoil more and turn the alpha particles back less.

explanation: The repulsion is proportional to the nuclear charge Ze. With Z = 13 instead of 79, close encounters produce smaller deflections, so fewer particles are scattered through large angles.
hints: What sets the size of the repulsive force?

stem: Estimate the mass of a nucleus of iron-56, taking each nucleon to have a mass of $1\ \text{u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$. Give your answer in kg to three significant figures.
explanation: $m \approx 56 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} = 9.30 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg}$. Using only the 26 protons ignores the neutrons, which have almost the same mass.
workedSolution: 1. $m \approx 56 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} = 9.30 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg}$. Using only the 26 protons ignores the neutrons, which have almost the same mass.

stem: An atom of radius $1.2 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ has a nucleus of radius $5.0 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$. Treating both as spheres, calculate the ratio volume of atom ÷ volume of nucleus, to two significant figures.
explanation: Volume scales as $r^3$: $\left(\dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-10}}{5.0 \times 10^{-15}}\right)^3 = (24000)^3 = 1.4 \times 10^{13}$. The ratio of radii alone (about $2.4 \times 10^{4}$) is not the volume ratio.
workedSolution: 1. Volume scales as $r^3$: $\left(\dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-10}}{5.0 \times 10^{-15}}\right)^3 = (24000)^3 = 1.4 \times 10^{13}$. The ratio of radii alone (about $2.4 \times 10^{4}$) is not the volume ratio.

stem: An aluminium-27 nucleus has a radius of $3.6 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$. Taking the mass of each nucleon as $1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$, calculate the density of the nucleus in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, to two significant figures.
explanation:
1. $m = 27 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} = 4.48 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg}$.
2. $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(3.6 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 1.95 \times 10^{-43}\ \text{m}^3$.
3. $\rho = m/V = 2.3 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, about $10^{14}$ times the density of aluminium metal. Nuclear matter has roughly the same density in every nucleus.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $m = 27 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27} = 4.48 \times 10^{-26}\ \text{kg}$.
2. $V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi(3.6 \times 10^{-15})^3 = 1.95 \times 10^{-43}\ \text{m}^3$.
3. $\rho = m/V = 2.3 \times 10^{17}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, about $10^{14}$ times the density of aluminium metal. Nuclear matter has roughly the same density in every nucleus.
hints: Use V = 4πr³/3 with the radius, not the diameter.

stem: A fully ionised lead atom ${}^{208}_{82}\text{Pb}$ (a bare nucleus) is accelerated in a particle accelerator. Taking its mass as $208\ \text{u}$, calculate its charge-to-mass ratio in $\text{C kg}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.
hints: The charge depends on Z, the mass on A.

stem: In a modern version of the scattering experiment, a detector at $30^\circ$ records the following counts in four 10-minute intervals: 412, 386, 431, 398. Using half the range as the absolute uncertainty, calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean count, to two significant figures.
explanation: Mean $= 406.8$; half-range $= (431 - 386)/2 = 22.5$; percentage uncertainty $= 22.5/406.8 \times 100 = 5.5\%$. The counts vary because decay and scattering are random; longer counting times reduce the percentage uncertainty.
workedSolution: 1. Mean $= 406.8$; half-range $= (431 - 386)/2 = 22.5$; percentage uncertainty $= 22.5/406.8 \times 100 = 5.5\%$. The counts vary because decay and scattering are random; longer counting times reduce the percentage uncertainty.

stem: Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their neutral atoms.
explanation: True. Chemistry depends on the electrons; isotopes have the same Z, hence the same number of electrons, but different numbers of neutrons.

stem: The unified atomic mass unit is defined as the mass of one proton.
explanation: False. 1 u is one twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom (1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg). A proton is slightly heavier, 1.007 u.

stem: Match each particle with its charge.
explanation: Proton +e, neutron uncharged, electron −e, alpha particle (two protons, two neutrons) +2e.

stem: Complete the statements about nuclide notation.

payload.template: In the symbol for a nuclide, the upper number is the {{blank:a}} number and the lower number is the {{blank:b}} number. The number of neutrons is found by {{blank:c}} the lower number from the upper number.

explanation: A (nucleon number) on top, Z (proton number) below; neutrons = A − Z.

stem: Describe the main results of the alpha-particle scattering experiment.

points.description: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil (undeflected or deflected by small angles).
A small number were deflected through large angles.
A very small number (about 1 in 10 000 or fewer) were deflected through more than 90° (came back).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Nearly all the alpha particles went straight through the gold foil or were deflected only slightly. A few were deflected through large angles, and a very small fraction, of the order of 1 in 10 000, bounced back through more than 90°.

explanation: Three observations, from most to fewest.

stem: Explain how the results of the alpha-particle scattering experiment lead to the conclusion that an atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

points.description: Most particles undeflected: most of the atom is empty space (nothing to repel them).
Large-angle deflections: the positive charge is concentrated in a very small region, giving a very strong repulsive force close to it.
Rebounds: that small region contains most of the mass of the atom (a light object could not reverse a fast alpha particle).
Few particles deflected strongly: only those passing very close to the nucleus, so the nucleus is very small compared with the atom.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Because most alpha particles pass straight through, most of the atom must be empty. Large deflections need a strong repulsion, which requires the positive charge to be concentrated in a tiny region. Some particles bounce back, so that region must also hold most of the mass; electrons are far too light to do this. Since only a very small fraction is strongly deflected, few particles pass close enough, so the nucleus is tiny compared with the atom.

explanation: Pair each observation with its conclusion.
hints: Link each observation to one property of the nucleus.

stem: State two features of the experimental arrangement in the alpha-particle scattering experiment and give a reason for each.

points.description: The apparatus is evacuated, because alpha particles are absorbed by a few centimetres of air.

The foil is very thin, so each alpha particle is scattered by at most one nucleus (or: a narrow, parallel beam, so the scattering angle is well defined; or: gold, because it can be made very thin and has massive, highly charged nuclei).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The chamber is evacuated because alpha particles travel only a few centimetres in air. The foil is extremely thin so that each alpha particle interacts with at most one nucleus, which makes the scattering pattern easy to interpret.

explanation: Vacuum, thin foil, narrow beam, gold.
hints: Think about the range of alpha particles.

stem: Four nuclides are: ${}^{12}_{6}\text{C}$, ${}^{14}_{6}\text{C}$, ${}^{14}_{7}\text{N}$ and ${}^{16}_{8}\text{O}$. Carbon-14 is formed in the upper atmosphere when a neutron is absorbed by a nitrogen-14 nucleus, which then emits a particle Y.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the two nuclides that are isotopes of each other (give their symbols, e.g. C-12 and C-14).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: State the number of neutrons in a nitrogen-14 nucleus.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the charge on an oxygen-16 nucleus, in C, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Complete the equation ${}^{14}_{7}\text{N} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{14}_{6}\text{C} + \text{Y}$ by naming Y.
parts.explanation: Top: 14 + 1 = 14 + A, A = 1. Bottom: 7 + 0 = 6 + Z, Z = 1. Y is a proton.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State the two quantities that are conserved in the reaction in (d), and show that they balance.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Nucleon number is conserved: 14 + 1 = 14 + 1 = 15. Charge is conserved: 7 + 0 = 6 + 1 = 7.

explanation: Isotopes share Z; neutrons = A − Z; charge = Ze; balance top and bottom numbers.
hints: Isotopes have the same proton number.

stem:
In an alpha-particle scattering experiment, the numbers of alpha particles detected in equal times at different angles $\theta$ are:

| $\theta\,/\,^\circ$ | number detected |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | 4200 |
| 30 | 52 |
| 60 | 4 |
| 90 | 1 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how the number detected varies with angle, and what the trend shows about the size of the nucleus.

points.description: The number falls very steeply as θ increases (but is never zero).
Large deflections need a close approach to the nucleus; few particles come that close, so the nucleus is very small compared with the atom.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The count falls very rapidly with increasing angle but does not reach zero. A large deflection needs a very close approach to a nucleus, and only a tiny fraction of particles pass that close, so the nucleus must be very small compared with the atom.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which change would increase the number detected at 90°?

options.content: using a foil of a metal with a smaller proton number
options.rationale: Weaker repulsion gives fewer large deflections.

options.content: using alpha particles with greater kinetic energy
options.rationale: Faster particles are deflected less.

options.content: using a foil of a metal with a larger proton number
options.rationale: Correct: stronger repulsion near each nucleus.

options.content: filling the chamber with air
options.rationale: Air absorbs the alpha particles.

parts.explanation: The repulsive force is proportional to Ze.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the detector counts must be taken over long times at large angles.

points.description: Scattering (and emission) is random and the counts at large angles are very small.
A small count has a large percentage (random) uncertainty, so a long time is needed to get a count large enough to be reliable.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The process is random and very few particles are scattered through large angles, so short counts would be tiny with a large percentage uncertainty. Counting for longer gives larger totals and a smaller percentage uncertainty.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why the experiment uses a narrow beam rather than a wide one.

points.description: So the direction of the incident particles is well defined and the scattering angle can be measured accurately.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A narrow, parallel beam has a well-defined direction, so the angle through which each particle is scattered can be measured.

explanation: Steep fall with angle: small nucleus; larger Z gives more large-angle scattering; long counts reduce random uncertainty.
hints: How close must an alpha particle pass a nucleus to be turned through 90°?
